# Free triangle facet neutrality: exact noncanonical parameterization

This is an ordinary geometric rigidity lemma for a triangle, with a conditional mixed application. It removes the canonical-normal assumption from the free-source result when each of three caps isolates a different vertex. It does not assert that arbitrary data satisfying these equations are a globally critical mixed configuration.

## 1. Precise hypotheses and conclusion

Let K=conv(v_1,v_2,v_3) be a nondegenerate triangle. Let y have positive barycentric coordinates y_j with sum y_j=1. For j=1,2,3 let H_j be a closed halfplane through y containing v_j strictly and containing no other vertex strictly. Thus its intersection with edge v_jv_k is the initial segment from v_j of relative length t_jk in(0,1]. The value1 allows the boundary to pass through v_k; no vertex-contact case is silently excluded.

Let theta_j>0, sum theta_j=1, and beta>0. On each edge assume signed affine neutrality:

    integral_edge psi (sum_j theta_j 1_Hj-beta) ds=0
                      for every affine psi.                   (1)

Assume also the facet convex-potential stress

    integral_edge Phi (sum_j theta_j 1_Hj-beta) ds<=0
                    for every nonnegative convex Phi.         (2)

Then

    beta>=4/9.                                                (3)

Equality holds exactly when y is the centroid, theta_j=1/3, and all t_jk=2/3. In particular every cap boundary is parallel to its opposite triangle edge. All inequalities t_jk<1 follow from the hypotheses.

More precisely, all feasible data are parameterized by positive numbers r_1,r_2,r_3 satisfying

    r_1 r_2+r_1 r_3+r_2 r_3=1.                                (4)

Writing P=r_1+r_2+r_3 and R=r_1 r_2 r_3, the parameters are

    beta=(P-R)/(2P),
    theta_j=beta/(1+r_j^2),
    y_j=r_j(r_k+r_l)/2,
    t_jk=r_k(1+r_j^2)/(r_j+r_k).                               (5)

Conversely every positive triple satisfying(4) supplies caps and weights obeying(1),(2) at the point in(5). Thus the equality classification is sharp, and noncanonical neutral configurations with beta>4/9 really exist at the stated ordinary level.

## 2. Exact edge equations and endpoint hinges

The third cap, indexed l not in{j,k}, meets edge jk in at most boundary vertices, which have zero edge length. Parametrize that edge by x in[0,1] from v_j to v_k. Cap j occupies[0,t_jk], cap k occupies[1-t_kj,1]. The constant and affine tests in(1) give exactly

    theta_j t_jk+theta_k t_kj=beta,
    theta_j t_jk(1-t_jk)
             =theta_k t_kj(1-t_kj).                          (6)

For example the first moments about the midpoint of the edge are respectively -t_jk(1-t_jk)/2 and t_kj(1-t_kj)/2. This yields the second equation after cancelling the positive edge length.

An exposed nonnegative convex hinge supported on a sufficiently short interval next to vertex v_j has constant profile at least theta_j in its support. Applying(2) and shrinking that interval shows

    x_j:=theta_j/beta<=1.                                    (7)

This remains valid if some other cap contains that entire short interval; its nonnegative weight only strengthens the necessary inequality. Because theta_j>0, all x_j>0. The remainder of the necessity proof uses only(6),(7) and common-source geometry.

Define the nonnegative edge odds

    b_jk=(1-t_jk)/t_jk.

The equation of cap j in barycentric coordinates lambda is

    lambda_j-sum_(k!=j)b_jk lambda_k>=0.

Its boundary through the SAME y is therefore exactly

    y_j=sum_(k!=j)b_jk y_k.                                  (8)

Every row has at least one positive b_jk, since y_j>0.

## 3. Strictness of the normalized weights

If t_jk=1, the second equation in(6) forces t_kj=1, and the first becomes x_j+x_k=1.

For an edge with t_jk,t_kj<1, put b=b_jk>0,c=b_kj>0. Solving the two equations(6), divided by beta, gives

    x_j=c(1+b)^2/(b+c+2bc),
    x_k=b(1+c)^2/(b+c+2bc),
    1-x_j=b(1-bc)/(b+c+2bc),
    1-x_k=c(1-bc)/(b+c+2bc).                                 (9)

Now suppose x_j=1. An incident edge cannot have t_jk=1, because that would imply x_k=0. Thus both incident edges at j are strict. By(9), each neighboring x_k=1 and each product b_jk b_kj=1. Applying the same reasoning to k shows its other incident odds are also positive. Equation(8) then gives

    y_j>b_jk y_k>b_jk b_kj y_j=y_j,

a contradiction. Hence

    0<x_j<1 for every j.                                     (10)

This argument also covers possible vertex-contact edges elsewhere; it does not assume all cuts strict in advance.

## 4. The reciprocal-square parameterization

Put z_j=1-x_j>0 and

    r_j=sqrt(z_j/x_j)>0.

On a strict edge, equation(9) gives b_jk/z_j=b_kj/z_k=:sigma. Substitution back into(9) gives

    z_j z_k(sigma+1)^2=x_j x_k.

The positive square root is forced because sigma>0. Consequently

    b_jk=(r_j/r_k-r_j^2)/(1+r_j^2).                          (11)

If an edge has t_jk=t_kj=1, then x_j+x_k=1, whence r_j r_k=1, and formula(11) gives b_jk=b_kj=0. Thus(11) holds on EVERY edge, including all allowed contact branches.

Let

    T=sum_k y_k/r_k.

Substitute(11) into(8), multiply by1+r_j^2, and add the missing diagonal term. One obtains

    2y_j=r_j T-r_j^2.                                       (12)

Divide(12) by r_j and sum over j. Since sum y_j/r_j=T, this gives2T=3T-P, or T=P. Summing(12) without division and using sum y_j=1 gives

    2=P^2-sum_j r_j^2=2 sum_(j<k)r_j r_k.

This proves(4) and the formula for y in(5). In particular every r_j r_k<1, because the other two terms in(4) are positive. The contact case r_j r_k=1 is impossible. Thus all b_jk>0 and every t_jk<1 after all. Formula(11) gives precisely the cap fractions in(5).

Because theta_j=beta/(1+r_j^2) and sum theta_j=1,

    beta=1/[sum_j 1/(1+r_j^2)].                              (13)

Under(4), elementary symmetric expansion gives

    product_j(1+r_j^2)=(P-R)^2,
    sum_(j<k)(1+r_j^2)(1+r_k^2)=2P(P-R).

The denominator P-R is positive: each r_j r_k<1 implies, for example, R<r_1<P. Therefore(13) yields beta=(P-R)/(2P), with no denominator ambiguity.

## 5. Sharp constant and equality

For positive r_j,

    (r_1+r_2+r_3)(r_1r_2+r_1r_3+r_2r_3)>=9r_1r_2r_3.

Indeed after division by R its left side is

    3+sum_(j<k)(r_j/r_k+r_k/r_j)>=9,

using each reciprocal-pair inequality. By(4), P>=9R. Hence

    beta=1/2-R/(2P)>=1/2-1/18=4/9.

Equality forces every reciprocal pair equal, so r_1=r_2=r_3=1/sqrt3. Formula(5) gives y_j=1/3, theta_j=1/3, t_jk=2/3. Conversely these data plainly satisfy all edge equations and the convex stress. This is exactly the canonical centroid case.

## 6. Converse and full convex order on each edge

Take any positive r satisfying(4). Set the data by(5),(11). All b_jk>0, all t_jk in(0,1), y_j>0, and sum y_j=1. Equations(8) hold by reversing(12). The caps lambda_j-sum b_jk lambda_k>=0 therefore meet at y and each isolate vertex j.

They form a genuine positive continuous circuit. For z_j=r_j^2/(1+r_j^2), formula(11) makes b_jk/z_j symmetric in j,k. Equation(8) then implies that the positive vector rho_j=y_j/z_j is a left null vector of I-B, so the corresponding positive weighted sum of the three affine cap margins is identically zero. Their normals span the plane, since three distinct isolated vertices cannot be realized by only two opposite directions through one interior point.

Reversing(9) verifies(6), hence signed affine neutrality on every edge. Further,

    x_j+x_k>1,

because its difference from1 is

    [1-r_j^2 r_k^2]/[(1+r_j^2)(1+r_k^2)]>0.

The two captured edge intervals overlap properly. On that edge the profile minus beta is negative at the two ends (each x_j<1) and positive on their central overlap. Its total mass and first moment vanish by(6). Let l be the affine line through the values of any convex test Phi at the two overlap endpoints. Convexity gives Phi<=l inside that interval and Phi>=l on the two outer intervals. Thus pointwise

    (W-beta)(Phi-l)<=0.

Its integral is nonpositive, while integral(W-beta)l=0. This proves(2) for EVERY convex test, in particular every nonnegative convex test. No smoothness, hinge-density approximation or numerical test is needed.

As an exact noncanonical example, take r=(1/2,1/2,3/4). Then

    beta=25/56>4/9,
    theta=(5/14,5/14,2/7), y=(5/16,5/16,3/8),
    t_12=t_21=t_31=t_32=5/8,
    t_13=t_23=3/4.

The positive affine-margin circuit has coefficients(3,3,2). This illustrates the scope: these ordinary data satisfy full edge neutrality and convex stress, but their cap areas are not equal. No globally critical mixed realization is asserted.

## 7. Conditional mixed consequence

In the exact free-source/single-cover setting of
`candidate 00208e2b45f0da1a`, suppose the free source is a triangle and the regular positive three-cap circuit isolates its three vertices in the sense of Section1. Actual signed affine facet freedom at a local minimum gives(1); the full convex-potential stress supplies(2). The actual response weights theta include all proper coareas in all other fibers, whose regular cap statuses may be arbitrary. The theorem gives beta>=Gamma_2=4/9, hence rules out beta<Gamma_2/2^n under those hypotheses.

For several deepest witnesses, signed variations do not separately force each circuit neutral; for supporting coincidences the response weights require actual allocations; and for arbitrary cap incidence the three vertex-isolating edge equations need not hold. Those cases are not settled here.
